title: Indian Social Structure
summary: Indians have multiple identities based on region, language and religion, each with a distinct social structure. Tribe is one of the earliest identifiable social organisations: Munda, Ho, Oraon, Bhil, Gaddi, Santhal, Kol, Kandh, Khasi, Garo, Mizo and Naga are in the Schedule and are called Scheduled Tribes. Features of a tribe: all members are related by blood; equal in status; believe in descent from a common ancestor; equal access to resources; little sense of private property; social differentiation only by age and sex. A tribe is endogamous; a clan is exogamous. Vedic tribes: Bharatas, Yadus, Turvasas, Druhyus, Purus and Anus; the head was the Raja, first among equals; the main distinction was varna (colour); non-Vedic people were dasa varna (alien language, dark complexion, different gods).

Wars among tribes, subjugation of the vanquished, loot and unequal wealth turned the initial differentiation into the varna system: Brahmanas (priests), Kshatriyas (political functions), Vaishyas (agriculturists) and Shudras (servile class); the three upper varnas had the sacred thread (upanayana) and were dvijas (twice-born). Buddhism and Jainism ridiculed the system but did not end it (no caste within their monastic communities; Kshatriyas were highest in Buddhist view). New groups – Shakas, Kushanas, Parthians and Indo-Greeks – changed it; guilds (shreni) later became castes, with the shreshthins (Seths and Chettis) as bankers; between 500 BC and 500 AD the caste system crystallised; the number of castes grew with crafts, new groups, inter-caste marriages (anuloma and pratiloma) and inclusion of tribes; the Dharmashastras and Smritis fixed duties and relations were governed by endogamy, commensality and craft exclusiveness. In the 5th–7th centuries land grants turned Vaishyas into servile peasants and tribal cultivators became Shudras, so Vaishyas and Shudras were lumped together; in Bengal and the South mostly Brahmanas and Shudras remained; Rajputs emerged from the 7th century. The system was so entrenched that plants were divided by varna and house sizes prescribed by varna. In medieval South India Shudras were divided into pure and impure and into left-hand (idangai) and right-hand (velangai) castes; Manu noted 61 castes; Kayasthas (scribes) became a caste; Khatris, Gurjaras, Jats and Ahirs claimed Kshatriya origin; regional variations: Kanyakubja, Sarayuparin and Maithila Brahmanas; Rajput sub-castes with tribal names; Marathas became a caste. In modern times surnames were added and caste and anti-caste movements made new castes (Brahmo Samajis). Egalitarian reformers such as Basava, Ramananda and Kabir tried to abolish caste, but their sects became castes; Sikhs, Muslims and Syrian Christians of Kerala also developed caste features.

Untouchables (antyajas, the fifth varna or panchama; chandala) were outside Brahmanical society; the notion rooted in the late Vedic period and became a separate category in the Buddha's age; they lived outside villages, cremated corpses, wore the dead's garments, ate from broken vessels and iron ornaments, and by the Gupta period had to strike a wooden clapper on entering a town; nishadas (hunters), kaivartas (fishermen), charmakaras (leather workers), kukkusas (sweepers) and basket makers became untouchables; Mahatma Gandhi called them Harijans; untouchability is now a punishable crime, though it continues in rural areas. Slavery in India differed from Greek and Roman slavery (Megasthenes found none): a female slave who bore her master a son became free and the child had the master's son's status; the Arthashastra says a man could be a slave by birth, voluntary sale, capture in war or judicial punishment; slaves were domestic servants; the masters had no rights over their lives; Delhi Sultans kept bandagans (Malik Kafur became commander-in-chief); the Portuguese traded slaves at Goa; Lord Cornwallis attacked it; the slave trade is now prohibited.

Four aims of life (purusharthas): dharma (right conduct), artha (livelihood), kama (worldly desires) and moksha (salvation). Four ashramas (stages): brahmacharya (after upanayana; education with the guru, plain living and high thinking), grihastha (the most important; marriage, children, livelihood, duties to society), vanaprastha (retire to the forest, detachment, meditation) and sanyasa (complete renunciation). The scheme was an ideal and may have been evolved to counter Buddhism and Jainism. The stages begin not with physical birth but with the sacred thread ceremony; there are about forty samskaras (garbhadhana, pumsavana, simantonnayana, jatakarma, nishkramana, annaprashana, chudakarma, upanayana, samavartana, vivaha, antyeshti) prescribed for the three upper varnas. Jajmani system (early medieval, rural): a complementary relationship between dominant peasant castes and service and artisan castes (leather-workers, barbers, priests, garland makers, ploughmen, smiths) who got traditional shares of produce or plots of land; it is breaking up due to monetisation, urbanisation and industrialisation.

Joint family: two or more generations with a common hearth and jointly owned property, patriarchal and patrilineal (matrilineal in Kerala, Nagaland and Meghalaya); nuclear families in towns; members are bound by shraddha (sapindas). Law: Mitakshara (most of India) and Dayabhaga (Bengal and Assam); Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh and Jain families are governed by the Hindu Acts of 1955–56; Muslims, Christians and Parsis have their own personal laws. Marriage kinds: hypergamous (anuloma – high-caste man, low-caste woman) and hypogamous (pratiloma); by number of spouses – monogamous, polygamous and polyandrous (Draupadi; Khasas); arranged marriages within the caste but different gotras and pravaras (prohibited degrees: seven generations paternal and five maternal; not followed in the South where cousin marriages are accepted); polygamy was for alliances (Chandragupta, Akbar) and sons and is illegal now (Muslims may marry up to four with conditions); the Brahmanical law treated marriage as indissoluble after the seven steps. Women: in the Vedic period they took part in tribal affairs, composed hymns and chose husbands; later law books reduced them to Shudra status with only stridhana, closed Vedic knowledge; early marriage, sati, veil (brought by Arabs and Turks); reformers (Ram Mohan Roy, Radhakanta Deb, Bhawani Charan Banerji) got sati banned in 1829; infanticide declared murder (1895); first widow remarriage 1856 (Vidyasagar); Widow Marriage Association (1860); Hindu Marriage Act 1955 (minimum age 18 for the bridegroom and 15 for the bride, later raised); Supreme Court recognised a daughter's share in the father's property.

Tribes (adivasis, original inhabitants, the 'Fourth World') have roots in the soil, live in relative isolation in hills and forests, have a distinct culture, and their development needs priority. The Government has specified 427 communities as Scheduled Tribes with special protection; the three biggest are Gonds, Bhils and Santhals (over 30 lakh each); then Minas, Mundas and Oraons (over 5 lakh); 8.43 crore, 8.2% of the population (2001). Seven zones: North (Khasa – polyandrous, Tharu, Bhoksa, Bhotias – carpets and trade, Gujjars – pastoral, Jaunsaris; problems: inaccessibility, lack of communication, poverty, illiteracy, land alienation); North-East (Nagas, Khasi, Garo, Mishing, Miri, Karbi; problems: ecological degradation from shifting cultivation, inaccessibility, isolation and hostility to the mainstream); Central (maximum concentration; Santhals with the Ol Chiki script, Ho, Baiga – shifting cultivation, Muria, Munda, Birhor – near extinction; problems: land alienation, indebtedness); Southern (Toda – buffalo herding, Koya, Chenchu – hunting-gathering, Allars – cave and tree-top dwellers; problems: shifting cultivation, backwardness, isolation, language extinction); Eastern (Paraja, Kondhas, Bondas, Gadabas, Santals; problems: economic backwardness, exploitation by forest officials and contractors, land alienation, disease, displacement by industrial projects); Western (Bhils, Garasiya, Meenas – very advanced and educated); Islands (Great Andamanese, Jarwas, Onges, Nicobarese, Shompen – stone-age livelihood, threat of extinction, disease and malnutrition). The tribal sub-plan strategy began in the Fifth Five-Year Plan to eliminate exploitation, promote socio-economic development, bridge the development gap and improve quality of life.

vsa: Discuss the changes which came in Indian society during the Maurya and post-Mauryan period.

Urban centres, trade and crafts grew; guilds (shreni) became important and later castes; new groups (Shakas, Kushanas, Parthians, Indo-Greeks) arrived; Buddhism and Jainism challenged Brahmanism; the caste system started to crystallise and untouchability became a separate category.

or: Why did guilds become important during the Mauryan and post-Mauryan period?
They controlled craft production and trade, acted as bankers and trustees, provided technical education and had their own court and law (shreni-dharma).

vsa: Explain the beginning of untouchability in Indian society during ancient times.

The notion of purity and pollution led to the antyajas (outside Brahmanical society) taking root in the late Vedic period; it became a separate category in the Buddha's age, and groups like chandalas, hunters, fishermen, leather workers and sweepers became untouchables.

or: Explain the efforts made to abolish untouchability in the modern period.
Gandhi campaigned and called them Harijans; Ambedkar opened schools; the Constitution declared untouchability a punishable offence; education and social movements bridged the gap.

vsa: Examine any two specific features of the life of tribal people.

They live in relative isolation in hills and forests with roots in the soil; their language, institutions, beliefs and customs differ from others; members are equal and share resources with little private property.

or: How does a tribe become numerically important? Name one such tribe.
When its population is large – the Gonds, Bhils and Santhals each have more than 30 lakh.

vsa: Twice-born – members of the three upper varnas (Brahmana, Kshatriya and Vaishya) who were entitled to the sacred thread ceremony.
Write the problems of the tribal people of the Eastern zone.
Economic backwardness, exploitation by forest officials and contractors, land alienation, disease and displacement due to industrial projects.

A complementary relationship in rural society between dominant peasant castes and service and artisan castes who received fixed shares of produce or land for their services; it is breaking up due to monetisation and urbanisation.
A comprehensive strategy begun in the Fifth Five-Year Plan to end exploitation of tribals, promote their socio-economic development, bridge the development gap and improve quality of life.
sa: Discuss any three major problems of tribal people living in the North Zone of India.
Inaccessibility of their hilly areas, lack of communication and roads, poverty and illiteracy, and land alienation; the tribes include Khasa, Tharu, Bhoksa, Bhotias, Gujjars and Jaunsaris.

or: Discuss any three major problems of tribal people living in the North-East Zone of India.
Ecological degradation from shifting cultivation, inaccessibility and lack of communication, and isolation that created hostility to the mainstream.

sa: Explain three types of marriages based on the number of spouses.

Monogamy (one spouse at a time, the most common), polygamy (more than one wife, practised by kings and the rich, now illegal except for Muslims with conditions) and polyandry (more than one husband, as in the Khasas and in Draupadi's case, valid in some hill communities).

or: Explain the preconditions for arranged marriages among Hindus of India.
Parents arrange marriage within the same caste but of different gotras and outside the prohibited degrees (pravaras – seven generations paternal and five maternal).

sa: Explain the four purusharthas and ashramas.

The aims of life are dharma, artha, kama and moksha. For these a life is divided into brahmacharya (education), grihastha (family life and livelihood), vanaprastha (retirement and detachment) and sanyasa (renunciation).
Describe the institution of slavery in India.

Slavery differed from the Greek and Roman: a slave could be by birth, voluntary sale, capture or punishment; slaves were domestic servants and members of the household; masters had no rights over their lives; slave markets existed in Vijayanagara and the Portuguese traded slaves at Goa; Cornwallis attacked it and the trade is now prohibited.
Describe the position of women in the Vedic and post-Vedic periods.

In the Vedic period women took part in tribal affairs, composed hymns and chose husbands at a mature age; later law books reduced them to Shudra status, gave only stridhana, closed Vedic knowledge to them, and early marriage, sati and the veil became common.
la: Describe any five special features of tribals.

Tribals are among the oldest inhabitants (adivasis) with roots in the soil; they live in relative isolation in hills and forests; all members are related by blood, equal in status and descended from a common ancestor; they have equal access to resources and little private property; social differences exist only by age and sex; a tribe is endogamous and made of exogamous clans; they have a distinct language, institutions, beliefs and customs; development and protection need priority and 427 communities are Scheduled Tribes.

or: Early Vedic tribes were the Bharatas, Yadus, Turvasas, Druhyus, Purus and Anus with a Raja who was first among equals; the main distinction was between Vedic tribes and the dasa varna with alien language, dark complexion and different gods; this differentiation grew into the varna system.

la: Examine the evolution of the caste system in India.

From the tribal society with varna (colour) differences, wars, loot and unequal wealth produced the four varnas. Buddhism and Jainism ridiculed it but did not remove it. Guilds of craftsmen and traders became castes; new groups arrived; between 500 BC and 500 AD the system crystallised and castes multiplied with crafts, anuloma and pratiloma marriages and inclusion of tribes. After the 5th century Vaishyas and Shudras merged as peasants; in the south Shudras were pure and impure; Rajputs, Kayasthas and Marathas became castes; later surnames were added; reformers' sects and even Sikhs, Muslims and Christians developed caste features.
Critically examine the position of women in the history of Indian society.

It is the story of progressive decline. In the Vedic period women took part in tribal affairs and composed hymns; later law books gave them Shudra status and only stridhana, denied Vedic study, promoted early marriage, sati and the veil. Reformers and modern education led to the ban on sati (1829), widow remarriage (1856), the Hindu Marriage Act (1955) and daughters' property rights, improving their condition.
Discuss the family and marriage institutions in India.

The traditional family is the joint family under a patriarch, bound by shraddha and governed by Mitakshara or Dayabhaga; nuclear families are growing and matrilineal ones exist in Kerala and the North-East. Marriage is a samskara; there are anuloma and pratiloma alliances, and monogamy, polygamy and polyandry; arranged marriages are within the caste and outside the same gotra and pravara; divorce was once not allowed but is now legal on grounds like cruelty and desertion; personal laws differ by religion.
Explain the tribal zones of India and the problems faced by tribals.

India has seven zones: North (Khasa, Gujjars – inaccessibility, poverty), North-East (Nagas, Khasi – shifting cultivation, isolation), Central (Santhals, Ho, Baiga – land alienation, indebtedness), Southern (Todas, Chenchus – backwardness, language loss), Eastern (Paraja, Kondhas – exploitation, displacement), Western (Bhils, Meenas) and Islands (Jarwas, Onges – threat of extinction). The government has a tribal sub-plan since the Fifth Plan.
